name: Gummy smile Botox

angle.text: Botulinum toxin in the upper lip muscles is used by people who want less gum showing when they smile. The lowered lip line is visible within days and temporary, and many small trials have measured it.

summary: Botulinum toxin in the upper lip muscles to lower the lip line; temporary, with many small trials.
note: Effect is temporary (months) and gummy smile use is generally off-label.
currentQuick:
Botulinum toxin is injected into the muscles that raise the upper lip so less gum shows when smiling.
Wikipedia reports an average duration of roughly six months. Registered trials are mostly small and compare doses, sites and combinations with surgery.
How it works: The toxin blocks nerve signals to the targeted muscles, so the lip rises less on smiling.
Risks and caveats: General cosmetic effects described include weakness of nearby muscles, bruising and headache. It is a prescription product administered by clinicians, and effects wear off.
deepLead:
Botulinum toxin treatment for a gummy smile involves injecting the toxin into the muscles that lift the upper lip so the lip rises less on smiling and less gum shows. A gummy smile, or excessive gingival display, is commonly described as more than about 2 mm of gum visible above the upper front teeth when smiling.
Wikipedia describes the effect as lasting an average of about six months, and botulinum toxin cosmetic effects in general are temporary and require repeat treatment. Registered trials have compared injection sites and doses, EMG guidance, and combinations with surgery, though many are small.

name: Crown lengthening / gingivectomy

angle.text: Crown lengthening and gingivectomy reshape the gum line so teeth look longer and less gum shows, used for gummy smiles where the gum line is the cause. The change in tooth display is visible once healed.

summary: Dental surgery that trims gum (and sometimes bone) to expose more tooth, used for gummy smiles when the gum line is the cause.
note: Bone removal is irreversible and can affect adjacent teeth.
currentQuick:
Crown lengthening and gingivectomy remove gum tissue, and in some cases bone, to expose more of the teeth. They are standard periodontal procedures also used to reduce gum display in a smile.
Registered trials compare surgical, flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided methods.
How it works: Gum is trimmed or repositioned, with bone recontouring if needed, so the gum line sits higher on the teeth.
Risks and caveats: Described drawbacks include irreversible bone loss, weakening of neighbouring teeth, pain with flap surgery, recurrence and black triangles.
deepLead:
Crown lengthening exposes more tooth by removing gum tissue and sometimes supporting bone, and is done for functional or aesthetic reasons, including gummy smile. Gingivectomy is the removal of part of the gum tissue and is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy.
Both are established dental procedures used for restorative and periodontal reasons; their use for smile aesthetics is the part relevant to looksmaxxing. Registered trials in 2011-2026 compare techniques such as flapless, piezoelectric, laser and digitally guided approaches.

name: Lip repositioning surgery

angle.text: Lip repositioning is used for gummy smiles caused by a hypermobile upper lip, limiting how far the lip rises on smiling. The reduced gum display is visible after healing.

summary: Surgery that shortens the upper lip vestibule so the lip rises less, aimed at gummy smiles from a hypermobile lip.
note: Evidence is mostly case series and small studies; relapse is a studied outcome.
currentQuick:
Lip repositioning surgery removes a strip of mucosa inside the upper lip and re-attaches it higher, restricting how far the lip lifts when smiling.
A 2021 meta-analysis measured gum display reduction; the evidence base is mainly case series and small trials.
How it works: Reducing the depth of the vestibule limits the upward movement of the lip and may increase lip fullness.
Risks and caveats: It is an elective surgical procedure; reviews and trials examine relapse and technique variations such as myotomy.
deepLead:
Lip repositioning surgery (LRS) is a procedure for excessive gingival display, or gummy smile, in which strips of mucosa are removed from the inside of the upper lip and the lip is reattached in a more coronal position, limiting how far it rises on smiling. It is used particularly when a hypermobile upper lip is a cause.
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis quantified short- and long-term reduction in gum display after LRS and examined the effect of myotomy. Evidence includes case series, small trials and reviews.

name: Gum contouring laser

angle.text: Laser gum contouring is used to even out the gum line and show more tooth, as a laser version of gingivectomy. The reshaped gum line is visible after healing, with little direct study of the laser itself.

summary: Laser removal of gum tissue to reshape the gum line; a laser variant of gingivectomy with little direct study.
note: Benefits over scalpel are based on limited evidence.
currentQuick:
A dental laser trims gum tissue to change the gum line. It is a laser version of gingivectomy.
The source material is thin; claims of less pain and bleeding rest on limited evidence.
How it works: The laser vaporizes and cuts soft tissue while sealing small vessels.
Risks and caveats: High energy settings were linked to scarring and delayed healing in animal studies.
deepLead:
Laser gum contouring reshapes the gum line using a dental laser to remove soft tissue, a form of laser gingivectomy. Wikipedia lists Nd:YAG, CO2 and diode lasers among those used, and notes proposed benefits such as a bloodless field and minimal discomfort, based on limited evidence.
Few registered studies address it directly. One compares Er:YAG-assisted laser crown lengthening with surgical crown lengthening, and another examined wound-healing growth factors after soft tissue crown lengthening.

name: Enamel reshaping / contouring

angle.text: Enamel reshaping is used for quick, subtle fixes to uneven edges, chips and slightly long or pointed teeth, mostly on front teeth. The change is visible straight away.

summary: Shaving tiny amounts of enamel to even out edges and chips: quick and subtle, but permanent.
note: Enamel does not regenerate, so removal cannot be undone.
currentQuick:
Enamel reshaping is a dental procedure where a small amount of enamel is filed away to smooth chips, even out edges or slightly change the length or shape of a tooth, mostly on the front teeth.
It is usually described as a quick, single-visit treatment that often needs no anaesthetic. It is discussed in cosmetic dentistry as a subtle change, not a fix for major alignment problems.
How it works: A dentist uses fine instruments such as diamond burs, discs, strips or lasers to remove a thin layer of enamel, then polishes the surface.
Risks and caveats: Enamel does not grow back, so the change is permanent. Taking off too much can expose dentin and cause temporary sensitivity. No clinical studies specific to the procedure were found.
deepLead:
Enamel reshaping, also called enamel contouring, enameloplasty or odontoplasty, is a cosmetic dental procedure in which a dentist removes a small amount of the outer surface of a tooth to change its shape, length or edge, or to smooth chips and minor irregularities . It is typically applied to front teeth.
Descriptions of the procedure say it is quick, often completed in a single visit, and that enamel contains no nerve endings, so anaesthesia is frequently unnecessary . Because enamel does not regenerate, the change is permanent, and removing too much can expose the underlying dentin .
No clinical studies specific to the procedure were located for this article; the available descriptions come from general encyclopedic sources on cosmetic dentistry, one of which notes that parts of its own material rest on dental-practice and consumer websites .

name: Dental implants

angle.text: Dental implants are used to replace missing teeth with a fixed, natural-looking result. Forum posters also speculate about thickening the jaw or building up a recessed chin with implants and grafts; that jaw-reshaping use is not shown in studies.

summary: Titanium tooth roots with decades of survival data, but they replace teeth and aren't shown to reshape the jaw.
note: Evidence is for tooth replacement; forum hopes of jaw thickening or chin changes are untested.
currentQuick:
A dental implant is a titanium or zirconia post placed in the jawbone to hold a crown, bridge or denture. It is a standard way to replace missing teeth.
On looksmaxxing forums, users mostly ask whether implants and bone grafts can change jaw thickness or chin projection. Reference sources describe implants as tooth replacements and do not describe such effects.
How it works: The implant bonds to bone through osseointegration, then supports a prosthetic tooth after healing. Rough surfaces and coatings are designed to speed bone attachment.
Risks and caveats: Reported survival is about 93 to 98 percent at five years or more in healthy tissue. Complications include infection, loosening, fracture, nerve injury and peri-implantitis (bone loss around the implant), more likely with smoking, poor hygiene and diabetes.
deepLead:
A dental implant is a prosthetic fixture, most often made of titanium or zirconia, that is anchored in the jaw bone to support a crown, bridge or denture. Modern implants rely on osseointegration, a close bond between bone and the implant material . They are used mainly to replace missing teeth.
In looksmaxxing forums, implants are mostly discussed as a way to fill gaps, and occasionally with the question of whether an implant plus bone grafting can thicken or reshape the jaw. Encyclopedic sources describe implants as tooth-replacement devices and do not describe them as changing facial or jaw shape .
Survival rates in healthy tissue are reported at roughly 93 to 98 percent at five years or more, with complications such as peri-implantitis and mechanical problems reported over longer follow-up .

name: Crowns and bridges

angle.text: Crowns restore damaged teeth and bridges fill gaps from missing teeth, so the smile looks complete and uniform. The restored look is visible once fitted, and the methods are long established.

summary: Caps and fixed bridges that rebuild damaged or missing teeth; well-established, but they cost you tooth structure.
note: Tooth preparation is irreversible; restorations typically need replacement after about 10 years.
currentQuick:
A crown is a cap that covers a damaged or discoloured tooth. A bridge replaces missing teeth by anchoring an artificial tooth to neighbouring teeth or implants.
They are standard restorative dentistry and are also used cosmetically to improve the look of teeth that whitening or bonding cannot fix.
How it works: The tooth is shaped, an impression or digital scan is taken, and a restoration made from metal, porcelain or zirconia is cemented on, often designed and milled with CAD/CAM systems.
Risks and caveats: Preparation permanently removes tooth structure. Reported problems include decay at the margins, porcelain chipping, debonding, gum irritation, wear of opposing teeth and nickel allergy. Typical survival is reported at about 90 to 95 percent over 5 to 10 years.
deepLead:
A dental crown is a cap that covers or encircles a tooth or implant to restore its shape, strength and appearance, while a dental bridge is a fixed prosthesis that replaces one or more missing teeth by attaching an artificial tooth (pontic) to neighbouring teeth or implants .
Crowns are used for badly broken or worn teeth, to strengthen heavily restored teeth, and to improve the look of teeth that simpler cosmetic procedures cannot fix . Common materials include gold and other metal alloys, porcelain-fused-to-metal, all-ceramic and zirconia .
General references report high medium-term survival for modern restorations, with typical complications including decay at margins, porcelain chipping and debonding . Preparing a tooth for a crown involves permanent removal of tooth structure .

name: Smile makeover / digital smile design

angle.text: A smile makeover bundles whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns, gum contouring and orthodontics into one planned redesign, often previewed with digital smile design. The new smile is visible once the work is complete.

summary: A planned bundle of cosmetic dental work designed around the whole smile, previewed digitally first; pricey and mostly irreversible.
note: Tooth reduction for veneers and crowns is irreversible; design guidelines are conventions, not tested standards.
currentQuick:
A smile makeover is a planned set of cosmetic dental treatments, such as whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns or gum contouring, chosen to change how the teeth and gums look as a whole.
Digital smile design is the planning step, where photos and software (or wax mock-ups) preview the proposed look and apply proportion guidelines such as tooth width-to-length ratios.
How it works: Clinicians assess facial features, tooth display, tooth proportions and the gum line, then combine procedures to match a design. Restorations may be produced with CAD/CAM systems.
Risks and caveats: Veneers and crowns usually require permanent removal of tooth structure. Cosmetic dentistry is not an ADA-recognised specialty and critics raise overtreatment and marketing concerns. No clinical studies specific to smile makeovers were found.
deepLead:
A smile makeover is a planned, often multi-step programme of cosmetic dental work aimed at changing the colour, shape, size, alignment and display of the teeth and gums as a whole. It may combine procedures such as whitening, bonding, veneers, crowns, gum contouring and orthodontics .
Smile design refers to the planning stage, in which a clinician assesses facial features, tooth proportions, how much tooth shows at rest and during a smile, and the gum line. Digital smile design uses photographs and software to preview proposed changes; dentists have also long used wax or temporary mock-ups for the same purpose .
Cosmetic dentistry is not recognised as a specialty by the American Dental Association, and evidence on the design guidelines and on outcomes of whole-smile programmes is largely descriptive. No clinical studies specific to smile makeovers or digital smile design were located for this article .

name: Smile training / smile mirror practice

chain: More attractive smile in person and photos
angle.text: People practise smiling in a mirror or on camera to find a more natural, flattering expression for daily life and photos. It is free to try, and no trials of the practice itself were located.

summary: Rehearsing your smile in a mirror: free and harmless, but no trials test it for looks.
note: Facial feedback research is mixed and does not test attractiveness.
currentQuick:
Smile training means practising a smile, often in a mirror or on camera, to make it look more natural or appealing. It is a behavioural practice with no formal protocol.
No studies have tested it for appearance. Nearby research covers smile types and whether making facial expressions affects mood.
How it works: People practise controlling facial muscles, for example engaging the eye muscles as in a Duchenne smile. Facial feedback research asks whether expressions feed back on emotion; effects reported are small and contested.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms were found for the practice itself. Evidence for benefits to attractiveness is absent.
deepLead:
Smile training, or smile mirror practice, refers to deliberately rehearsing a smile, typically in front of a mirror or camera, with the aim of making it look more natural or attractive. No formal protocol or published trial of the practice itself was located for this article.
Related science exists on smile types and on the facial feedback hypothesis, the idea that facial expressions can influence emotional experience. A 2016 multi-lab replication did not reproduce a classic 1988 finding, while a later meta-analysis reported a small effect overall .

name: Smile maxxing

angle.text: Smile maxxing is a community umbrella term for improving the smile through whitening, alignment, cosmetic dentistry, gum and lip work, or better expression. It has no formal definition, and no published research uses the term.

summary: Forum shorthand for optimising your smile, from teeth to expression; a loose umbrella with no formal protocol.
note: An umbrella term; risks depend on whether it means dental procedures or expression practice.
currentQuick:
Smile maxxing is a looksmaxxing term for improving how your smile looks. It can mean dental changes such as whitening or alignment, or practising how the smile is expressed.
There is no formal definition or research using the term; it overlaps with cosmetic dentistry and smile training.
How it works: Dentally, it involves procedures that change tooth colour, shape and position. Expressively, it concerns which facial muscles are used, for example whether a smile engages the eyes (Duchenne smile).
Risks and caveats: Risks depend on the method. Dental procedures such as veneers can involve irreversible tooth reduction, while expression practice carries little reported risk. No studies of the term itself were found.
deepLead:
Smile maxxing is a looksmaxxing-community term for optimising how one's smile looks, whether through teeth (whitening, alignment, cosmetic dentistry), the gums and lips, or the way the smile is expressed. Sources reviewed for this article contain no formal definition of the term, and no published research uses it.
Related topics have encyclopedic coverage: the muscles and types of smile, the perception of smiling people, and cosmetic dental procedures .

name: Snap-on smile

angle.text: Users wear snap-on smile appliances to get an instantly even, bright-looking set of front teeth while the appliance is in. The visible change is immediate, and dental literature describes it as a temporary esthetic option documented in case reports rather than trials.

summary: A removable snap-over smile appliance from DenMat; documented in dental case reports as a temporary fix, with no trials behind it.
note: Evidence is case reports only; designed as a provisional appliance.
currentQuick:
Snap-On Smile is a thin removable appliance that fits over the existing teeth to change how the smile looks. It is a branded dental product, and the term is also used loosely online for removable fake veneers.
The published literature is made up of dentists' case reports, mostly on older or medically complex patients, enamel disorders and implant provisionals.
How it works: The appliance is a tooth-borne overdenture, reported to be made from acetal resin, that covers the teeth without altering them.
Risks and caveats: No trials have assessed it. Reports note the teeth can look too large in people with high smile lines or altered gums. It is described as temporary.
deepLead:
Snap-On Smile is a removable cosmetic dental appliance made by the dental company DenMat. It is a thin tooth-borne overdenture that fits over a person's existing teeth, and is described in the dental literature as a temporary esthetic option rather than a permanent restoration . In appearance culture, the term is also used generically for removable "fake veneers" that snap over the natural teeth.
Dentists have written about it mainly in case reports: for older patients with failing dentition and jaw disease, for people with the hereditary enamel disorder amelogenesis imperfecta, and as a provisional restoration during implant treatment . These publications are clinician-authored case descriptions and do not include controlled trials.

name: Fake tooth caps / press-on veneers

chain: Better-looking smile in photos and person
angle.text: Press-on veneers are used to change the apparent shape or shade of the teeth for a more even, brighter smile, with the change visible as soon as they are placed. No studies on these non-prescription covers have been published.

summary: DIY removable covers for the teeth; no studies on them exist.
note: No published research on these over-the-counter products.
currentQuick:
These are removable cosmetic shells placed over the front teeth to change how they look. They are not the same as dentist-made bonded veneers.
No published studies on the retail products were found.
How it works: The shell sits over the natural teeth, usually without bonding or tooth preparation.
Risks and caveats: Safety and fit have not been studied in published research; professional veneer literature does not cover these products.
deepLead:
Press-on veneers and fake tooth caps are non-prescription cosmetic covers that are placed over the front of the teeth to change their apparent shape or shade, and are usually removable. They differ from dental veneers, which are thin layers of composite or porcelain bonded to the tooth by a dentist .
Published research specifically on over-the-counter press-on products was not found. Background on professional veneers comes from general references.

name: DIY braces with rubber bands / paperclips

angle.text: People discuss improvised bands and bent wire as a low-cost way to straighten teeth without orthodontic treatment, aiming for a straighter smile. The idea rests on anecdote and home attempts; no research on the practice exists.

summary: Improvised home tooth-moving with bands or wire; no research exists on it.
note: Unsupervised; no published studies.
currentQuick:
People discuss moving teeth at home with household rubber bands or wire as a cheap substitute for braces.
No published research examines the practice.
How it works: Improvised bands or wire are meant to apply force to teeth; professional braces apply controlled forces that clinicians adjust over months [1].
Risks and caveats: Not studied. The orthodontic reference describes decay risk and relapse even in supervised treatment [1].
deepLead:
DIY braces refers to attempts to move teeth at home using improvised materials such as rubber bands or bent wire, without a clinician's supervision. It is discussed as a low-cost alternative to orthodontic treatment.
No published studies of the practice were found. Professional orthodontics, by contrast, relies on brackets, wires and elastics adjusted by clinicians, typically every 4 to 10 weeks .

name: DIY gap bands

angle.text: Users place small elastic bands around front teeth hoping to close a gap (diastema) and get a more uniform smile without a dentist. The appearance benefit is based on personal accounts, and no studies on the method exist.

summary: Home elastic bands aimed at closing tooth gaps; no studies exist.
note: Unsupervised; no published studies.
currentQuick:
People try to close gaps between teeth by placing small elastic bands around them at home.
No research on the practice was found.
How it works: The band is intended to apply inward force; in clinics, such forces are applied by supervised appliances [1].
Risks and caveats: Not studied in published research.
deepLead:
DIY gap bands are small elastic bands that people place around teeth at home in an attempt to close the gap between front teeth (a diastema) without seeing a dentist.
No published studies of the home practice were found. Professional orthodontics uses elastics and springs as part of supervised appliances .

name: Chewing hard foods for jaw

angle.text: Forum posters chew tough or hard foods to build the masseter muscles and get a more defined jawline. The idea draws on the general principle that muscles grow with load, but its effect on facial appearance is untested.

summary: Chewing tough foods to bulk up the jaw muscles; untested for looks, with a possible jaw-joint association.
note: Reference sources list hard-food chewing among habits linked to jaw disorders, with limited evidence.
currentQuick:
Some people chew hard or tough foods hoping to enlarge the jaw muscles and sharpen the jawline.
No studies were found testing this for appearance.
How it works: The masseter can enlarge with habitual heavy use such as clenching or constant gum chewing [1].
Risks and caveats: Hard-food chewing is listed among habits suggested to be associated with temporomandibular disorders, though evidence is limited [2].
deepLead:
Chewing hard foods for the jaw is a practice in which people chew tough or hard items, with the aim of building the masseter muscles and a more defined jawline. Proponents tie it to the belief that chewing grows the jaw muscles.
The masseter is a strong chewing muscle, and habitual clenching, grinding or constant gum chewing can enlarge it . No studies were found testing hard-food chewing as a way to change facial appearance.

name: Jawline exerciser (Jawzrsize)

angle.text: Jawline exercisers like Jawzrsize are marketed to users who want stronger jaw muscles and a more defined jawline. The pitch borrows from muscle-training logic, and no studies on the product or its effect on facial appearance exist.

summary: A resistance chewing device marketed for jaw definition; no studies on the product exist.
note: No studies of the device; repetitive jaw habits are linked to jaw disorders in limited evidence.
currentQuick:
Jawline exercisers are devices you bite against to work the chewing muscles, sold as a way to define the jaw.
No published research on the products was found.
How it works: Resistance chewing loads the masseter, which can enlarge with habitual heavy use [1].
Risks and caveats: Repetitive jaw habits are suggested to be associated with jaw disorders, with limited evidence [2].
deepLead:
Jawline exercisers such as Jawzrsize are handheld devices that users bite or chew against with resistance, marketed to strengthen the jaw muscles and define the jawline.
No studies of these devices were found. Background research shows the masseter can enlarge with habitual heavy use , and that repetitive jaw habits have been suggested to contribute to jaw disorders, with limited evidence .

name: Orthodontic extractions debate

chain: Change in tooth alignment and profile
angle.text: Looksmaxxers follow this debate because orthodontic choices shape both the smile and the facial profile. One camp holds extractions flatten the face and favours expansion; orthodontic history shows both approaches in use, and the facial-effect claims remain contested.

summary: The long-running split over pulling teeth to straighten the rest, now amplified online by the anti-extraction orthotropic narrative.
note: Orthodontists and orthotropic proponents disagree; decisions are case-specific and made with a clinician.
currentQuick:
Orthodontists sometimes remove teeth, most often premolars, to relieve crowding or change the lip profile. Whether to do so has been argued since the early 1900s. In looksmaxxing circles the argument is usually framed around the claim that extractions shrink the jaws and flatten the face.
Mainstream orthodontics treats extraction as one option chosen case by case. Orthotropic proponents, following John Mew, regard extractions as potentially harmful to facial growth. The orthotropic view is not supported by mainstream professional bodies.
How it works: Extraction treatment removes teeth to create space so the remaining teeth can be aligned or retracted. Critics argue that this reduces the room for the tongue and the dental arches. Orthodontists point to the individual's crowding, bite and profile as the basis for choosing extraction or non-extraction plans.
Risks and caveats: Extractions are irreversible and carry general surgical risks. Non-extraction plans, such as expansion, also have limits and relapse risk. Community members often describe fear of a changed profile; published evidence on this is limited and contested.
deepLead:
The orthodontic extractions debate concerns whether teeth, usually premolars, should be removed to resolve crowding and improve the facial profile, or whether space should instead be created by other means such as arch expansion. It is one of the oldest disputes in orthodontics. Edward Angle and his followers strongly opposed extraction and believed ideal occlusion would also yield good facial aesthetics, while Charles Tweed and Raymond Begg reintroduced extraction in the 1940s and 1950s to improve aesthetics and the stability of results . Teeth are reportedly extracted in about half of cases today, most commonly premolars .
In looksmaxxing communities the topic is tied to orthotropics, a system founded by British orthodontist John Mew that argues malocclusion is largely environmental and postural. Mew held that extractions, fixed appliances with elastics and retractive headgear could harm facial growth . Mainstream professional orthodontists do not support orthotropics, and commentators have described the evidence for it as inadequate .

name: Invisalign attachments / chewies

angle.text: Aligner users encounter attachments and chewies as accessories that help clear aligners seat and rotate teeth, supporting a straighter smile over the course of treatment. Attachments are described in dental sources; chewies are informal and have little dedicated research.

summary: Small bonded bumps and rubbery bite cylinders that help clear aligners grip and seat; useful accessories with little dedicated research.
note: Attachments are placed by a clinician; chewies are an adjunct, and aligners overall have limits for some movements.
currentQuick:
Clear aligners are plastic trays that move teeth in stages. Two accessories come up constantly: attachments, which are small tooth-colored composite shapes bonded to teeth, and chewies, soft cylinders users bite on to press the tray fully onto the teeth.
Attachments are part of the treatment plan set by the clinician. Chewies are mostly discussed by patients as a way to help trays seat; sources reviewed give no dedicated trial of them.
How it works: Because plastic is less rigid than metal, attachments give the tray something to push against so it can rotate or pull down teeth. Chewies work by biting force pressing the tray against the teeth to close small gaps.
Risks and caveats: More attachments can make the aligners look less discreet. Aligners in general are considered less effective than braces for rotations, extrusion and front-to-back jaw discrepancies, and relapse is reported.
deepLead:
Attachments are small tooth-colored composite shapes bonded to certain teeth during clear aligner treatment. They help the aligner rotate or pull down teeth, since the plastic is less rigid than metal . Chewies are soft cylinders that wearers bite on to help seat an aligner; they are an informal accessory and are not covered in the encyclopedic sources reviewed.
Clear aligners typically move teeth about 0.25 to 0.33 mm per stage, are worn around 22 hours a day, and treatment averages about 13.5 months . A 2014 systematic review found study quality insufficient to determine effectiveness, and aligners are considered less effective than conventional braces for rotations, extrusion and jaw discrepancies .

name: Retainer wear nightly

angle.text: People who have finished braces or aligners wear retainers at night to keep the straight smile they paid for. Orthodontic sources describe a lifelong relapse risk, with over half of patients showing some reversion within ten years.

summary: Wearing a retainer at night after braces or aligners to hold teeth in place; orthodontic sources describe relapse risk as lifelong.
note: Wear schedules are set by the treating orthodontist.
currentQuick:
After teeth are moved, they tend to drift back toward their old positions. Retainers are worn to hold the corrected alignment, and many orthodontists advise nightly wear for years after full-time wear.
In looksmaxxing circles it is framed as the way to keep results from relapse after braces or aligners.
How it works: Retainers resist relapse forces from recoil of the periodontal fibres, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued growth. Removable types are worn at set times; fixed types are bonded behind the front teeth.
Risks and caveats: Poor cleaning can cause plaque, cavities and gum inflammation. Clear retainers worn while eating can trap sugary or acidic substances, and hot water can distort them. Grinding can break them quickly.
deepLead:
Retainers hold teeth in corrected positions after orthodontic treatment. Orthodontic sources state there is a lifelong risk of relapse because of periodontal fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued growth . More than 50% of patients show some reversion within 10 years .
Removable retainers include Hawley and vacuum-formed types; fixed retainers are wires bonded behind the front teeth. Vacuum-formed retainers are usually worn overnight, and the wear schedule is set by the orthodontist and may be fixed-term or indefinite . One overview suggests about six months of full-time wear followed by nighttime wear for many years .

name: Wisdom tooth removal

angle.text: Wisdom teeth are routinely removed when impacted, and some looksmaxxers also discuss removal as a way to protect front-tooth alignment or relate it to jaw development. The crowding link is disputed among clinicians, and the jaw-shape link is based on forum theory.

summary: Surgical extraction of third molars, a routine procedure that looksmaxxers debate when it comes to crowding and jaw development.
note: Evidence that wisdom teeth cause crowding is not established; nerve injury is a recognised risk.
currentQuick:
Wisdom teeth, the third molars, usually erupt between about 17 and 21. When they lack room they can become impacted and are commonly removed to treat or prevent decay, gum infection or pain.
On forums, the topic turns on whether to remove them in people pursuing jaw expansion or worrying about crowding. Clinical guidance does not support crowding as a settled reason for removal.
How it works: Removal is an oral surgery procedure, often with a flap and bone removal for impacted teeth. Postoperative swelling and pain are the common sequelae studied in trials of drugs and techniques.
Risks and caveats: Removing lower third molars can damage the inferior alveolar nerve temporarily or permanently, reported in about 1 in 85 patients. Other risks include dry socket, swelling and infection.
deepLead:
Wisdom teeth are the rearmost molars and typically erupt between about 17 and 21 . They are the most commonly impacted teeth, and impaction can lead to decay, gum disease and pericoronitis . Impacted teeth are usually extracted to treat or prevent such problems, and some clinicians have also removed them to prevent orthodontic crowding, which is disputed .
Removal of disease-free impacted teeth has long been debated. The UK's NICE guidance (2000) opposes prophylactic removal, the American Public Health Association also opposes it, and a 2020 Cochrane review found evidence insufficient to settle the question . Research has found no agreed view that wisdom teeth cause lower incisor crowding .
